name: VIIRS annual nighttime lights as a time-varying pressure proxy

identity.method_name: VIIRS Day/Night Band (DNB) annual and monthly nighttime-radiance composites, plus a harmonized DMSP-OLS/VIIRS simulated annual series (1992-2023), used as a year-varying proxy for urbanisation/development pressure around each lake
identity.core_idea: The VIIRS DNB sensor records low-light radiance at night; cloud-, moon- and stray-light-affected observations are filtered out and the remainder averaged into cloud-free annual or monthly composite grids of radiance (nW/sr/cm^2) at roughly 464 m per pixel. Higher radiance broadly correlates with the presence and intensity of artificial lighting -- roads, buildings, commercial activity -- and so is proposed as a proxy for encroachment-adjacent development pressure that, unlike the project's static single-snapshot OpenStreetMap building count, genuinely takes a new value every year. A separate harmonized dataset extends a VIIRS-equivalent annual series back to 1992 by using a deep super-resolution model to simulate VIIRS-like radiance from the earlier, coarser DMSP-OLS sensor, giving one continuous, cross-calibrated series instead of two incompatible ones.
identity.official_dataset_ids: NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/ANNUAL_V22, NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG; and the harmonized simulated annual dataset published as: Chen, X., Wang, Z., Zhang, F., Shen, G., Chen, Q. (2024), 'A global annual simulated VIIRS nighttime light dataset from 1992 to 2023', Scientific Data 11, Article 1380, doi 10.1038/s41597-024-04228-6, data archived at https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.22262545.v8

fit_to_project.ground_truth_proxy_strategy: Unsupervised, descriptive data-source used as an additional covariate/feature, not as a substitute encroachment label. No labels are required to compute a radiance value, but the radiance value is not itself evidence of encroachment either -- it is, at best, a correlate of general 'urban pressure' in the vicinity of a lake, and using it as if it were validated encroachment evidence would overstate what it can show.
fit_to_project.input_required: A radiance grid clipped to each lake's surrounding area, aggregated to whatever spatial unit is actually resolvable (see resolution_match_20m below -- NOT the lake's own 30 m buffer). This is new data the project does not currently have and must acquire from Earth Engine (for the two official annual/monthly VIIRS products) or by downloading and reprojecting the figshare-hosted GeoTIFFs (for the harmonized 1992-2023 product, which is not natively an Earth Engine catalogue asset and would need to be uploaded as a user asset or read from the archive directly).
fit_to_project.viable_with_42_rows: Yes, but only as one or two additional columns on the existing 42-row lake-year table (e.g. mean annual radiance within a ward or catchment polygon per lake-year); it does not expand the row count the way a reframing to per-scene SAR observations would, because the underlying legal question this item is meant to speak to is fundamentally a SPATIAL resolution problem (see next fields), not a temporal-sampling one -- adding more monthly VIIRS composites densifies the time axis but does nothing to shrink the ~464 m pixel footprint down to the 30 m buffer scale.
fit_to_project.viable_without_ground_truth: yes, as a purely descriptive/explanatory covariate; no labels are needed to compute a radiance statistic.
fit_to_project.resolution_match_20m: No, and this is the central, disqualifying problem for this item at the scale the project actually needs. VIIRS DNB annual/monthly composites are delivered at approximately 463.83 m per pixel (confirmed on the official Earth Engine catalogue pages for both NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/ANNUAL_V22 and NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG), and the harmonized 1992-2023 dataset is likewise gridded at 500 m / 15 arc-seconds. That is roughly 23 times coarser per side, and about 530 times coarser in area, than the project's 20 m working grid, and it is dramatically coarser than the 30 m legal buffer distance the project is testing. Concretely: treating each lake as a circle of the stated size, a 30 m buffer ring around Sankey Tank (12.4 ha, ~350 m across) has an annulus area of only about 3.6 ha -- roughly one-sixth (about 17%) of the area of a single VIIRS pixel (~21.5 ha) -- and the lake plus its entire 30 m buffer together (~410 m across) is smaller than one VIIRS pixel's linear footprint (~464 m). Even for Bellandur, the largest lake in the study (315 ha, equivalent circular diameter ~2,003 m), the 30 m buffer ring's annulus area is only about 19 ha, still LESS than the area of a single VIIRS pixel (~21.5 ha). In other words, across the entire size range of this project's six lakes, the 30 m legal buffer never contains even one full, independently-resolved VIIRS pixel -- the honest answer to 'how many VIIRS pixels fall inside a 30 m buffer around these lakes' is zero to a fraction of one, for every lake in the study, including the largest. VIIRS nighttime lights therefore cannot say anything meaningful at buffer scale; the only scale at which it could plausibly carry signal is catchment or ward, several orders of magnitude larger in area than the buffer being tested.
fit_to_project.fixes_which_stated_limitation: Only limitation (2) (OpenStreetMap buildings are a static single snapshot with no year-to-year variation), and only if the project explicitly reframes its unit of analysis away from the 30 m buffer to a ward or catchment polygon -- at the buffer scale actually specified for this project, it fixes none of the four stated limitations, because the spatial mismatch computed above means there is no buffer-scale signal to be time-varying in the first place. It does not touch limitations (1), (3) or (4).
fit_to_project.handles_desilting_confound: No, not directly -- nighttime radiance measures human/artificial lighting activity, not water extent, and has no mechanism to distinguish a drained-for-desilting lake from an encroached one. At best, a rising ward-level radiance trend co-occurring with a declining water-area trend could be offered as weak, circumstantial corroborating context for a construction-driven (rather than desilting-driven) explanation, but this is suggestive narrative, not discriminating evidence, and only available at a spatial scale far coarser than the lake itself.
fit_to_project.handles_hyacinth_confound: No -- nighttime lights carry no information about the composition of a lake's water surface (open water vs. water hyacinth mat vs. any other vegetation) and are entirely unrelated to this confound.
fit_to_project.legal_traceability: None at the scale that matters. The 30 m distance the project is testing (traceable, depending on which regime is used, to the Karnataka Tank Conservation and Development Authority Act s.12(3)/its 2025 amendment, or to Bengaluru Master Plan language, as distinct from the now-largely-set-aside 75 m NGT figure) is precisely the scale the pixel-area calculation above shows VIIRS cannot resolve -- a legal buffer test needs to know what happens within tens of metres of a boundary, and VIIRS's native grid cannot distinguish 'inside the buffer' from 'several hundred metres away' at all. If used at all, it can only support a ward- or catchment-level narrative statement about general area-wide development pressure, with no claim of correspondence to the specific legal buffer line being adjudicated.
fit_to_project.temporal_granularity: This is the one dimension on which VIIRS is a genuine improvement over the project's current building data: annual composites are real, independently re-measured values each year (2012-2024 for the official VIIRS record; 1992-2023 for the harmonized/simulated series), not a constant repeated across years the way the single 2026 OpenStreetMap building snapshot is. The caveat is that this genuine year-to-year variation is only usable at the ward/catchment scale established above; at the lake-buffer scale there is no meaningful independent per-year measurement to be had, because the spatial unit itself does not resolve at that scale regardless of how many years of data exist.

implementation.libraries: Google Earth Engine Python API / `geemap` to read NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/ANNUAL_V22 and NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG directly from the Earth Engine catalogue; `pandas` and `rasterstats` or Earth Engine's own `reduceRegion`/zonal-statistics calls to aggregate radiance over ward or catchment polygons. The harmonized 1992-2023 dataset is not a native Earth Engine catalogue asset and would need to be downloaded from its figshare archive (doi 10.6084/m9.figshare.22262545.v8) and ingested manually with `rasterio`/GDAL, an added step beyond the two GEE-native products.
implementation.pretrained_weights: Not needed by the project, since only the harmonized dataset's OUTPUT rasters would be consumed, not its model retrained. The harmonized dataset's own super-resolution model (referred to in its documentation as an NTL super-resolution network trained on DMSP-OLS/VIIRS overlap years plus Landsat NDVI) was trained by its authors on global DMSP-VIIRS cross-calibration data at 500 m; whether its weights are separately released alongside the figshare data was not confirmed in this research pass [uncertain -- not required for this project's use case regardless, since only the published raster output is needed].
implementation.licence: VIIRS DNB data is produced by NOAA/the Earth Observation Group (Colorado School of Mines) and is public-domain/open (a U.S. government-associated product); Earth Engine catalogue access is free for research use. The harmonized dataset's figshare archive licence was not independently confirmed in this research pass [verify -- Scientific Data papers are typically published open-access with data under a permissive licence such as CC-BY, but this was not directly checked against the figshare record for this specific dataset].
implementation.compute_requirement: Trivial. Computing zonal (ward/catchment) mean radiance per lake-year is a lightweight reduceRegion/zonal-statistics operation over small rasters, runs in seconds on a laptop CPU or well within free Earth Engine quotas; no GPU is needed at any point.
implementation.student_days: Low mechanically (roughly 1 day to script annual/monthly zonal statistics for six areas across the study years) but with a real hidden cost: credible ward or catchment boundary polygons for the six lakes are not already part of the project's data (BBMP ward shapefiles would need to be sourced, or catchments delineated from a DEM via flow accumulation), which could add 2-3 more days; ingesting the non-native harmonized figshare product adds roughly another 0.5-1 day. All of this effort is spent producing a signal that, per the resolution analysis above, cannot speak to the 30 m buffer the project is actually testing -- so the honest framing is that most of this time would be spent on a descriptive, ward-level side-narrative rather than on evidence relevant to the project's central encroachment question.

evaluation.metrics: Only descriptive/correlational metrics are available -- e.g. a Pearson or Spearman correlation between a ward/catchment radiance trend and other lake-year features (water-area trend, building density change) -- since there is no ground truth for 'development pressure' any more than there is for encroachment. Accuracy-style metrics do not apply because there is no independently verified pressure label to score against.
evaluation.validation_protocol: If used as an additional covariate in the existing 42-row lake-year table, the same leave-one-lake-out protocol used elsewhere in the project applies; this item does not create a new sample-size regime of its own since it does not expand the row count (see viable_with_42_rows).
evaluation.leakage_risk: The most serious risk is specific to this item: all six lakes sit inside the same city and are exposed to the same city-wide nighttime-brightening trend, so a rising radiance signal measured near any one lake is likely to be substantially the SAME shared Bengaluru-wide trend rather than six independent, lake-specific pressure signals. Treating six correlated draws of one underlying city-level trend as if they were six independent per-lake observations would overstate the evidence for any lake-specific effect and is a genuine, easy-to-miss leakage risk in this specific item.
evaluation.uncertainty_reporting: No calibrated uncertainty is inherent to a radiance composite; if ward/catchment aggregates are used, a bootstrap over the set of contributing pixels (small in number, given the coarse resolution) could give a rough interval, but with so few independently-resolved pixels per ward/catchment for a compact study area, any such interval would itself be wide and should be reported as such rather than presented as a precise trend.
evaluation.augmentation_honesty_risk: Not applicable to the two official VIIRS products (they are direct measurements), but a specific honesty risk applies to the harmonized 1992-2023 dataset: its own documentation states that the pre-2012 portion is a MODEL-SIMULATED reconstruction from DMSP-OLS, not a direct VIIRS measurement, and that the underlying DMSP data 'suffers from interannual inconsistency, saturation, and blooming' while the simulation model itself 'tends to underestimate NTL intensity in urban core areas' and cannot fully recover dim-light pixels. Since the project's actual study window (2019-2025) falls entirely within the genuine VIIRS record (VIIRS DNB coverage begins April 2012), the harmonized product's simulated pre-2012 years are not even needed for this project, and using them at all -- e.g. to claim a longer pre-study baseline trend -- would require explicitly disclosing that those years are model output, not satellite measurement, and are documented by their own authors as less reliable in exactly the bright-urban-core and dim-fringe conditions most relevant to lake-adjacent land.

evidence.published_performance: The Earth Engine catalogue pages for NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/ANNUAL_V22 and NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG confirm a nominal spatial resolution of 463.83 m per pixel for both, and document that the annual product's 'annual' value is the twelve-month MEDIAN radiance (used specifically to discard high/low outliers such as fires), while the monthly VCMCFG product filters out data affected by stray light, lightning, lunar illumination and cloud cover before averaging, and is explicitly documented as NOT filtering aurora, fires, boats or other transient lights in this version. The harmonized dataset paper (Chen et al. 2024, Scientific Data 11:1380) reports a super-resolution cross-calibration approach (an 'NTL super-resolution network' trained on 2012-2013 DMSP/VIIRS overlap plus Landsat NDVI) to simulate VIIRS-equivalent radiance for 1992-2011, and states its own limitations of urban-core underestimation and imperfect dim-pixel recovery; the paper's exact quantitative validation statistics (e.g. R^2 or RMSE of the simulated-vs-real overlap years) were not retrieved in this research pass and should be checked directly against the paper before being quoted [verify]. General VIIRS DNB blooming/overglow behaviour (bright-source radiance visibly spreading into neighbouring pixels due to atmospheric scattering, the sensor point-spread function and stray light, typically discussed on the order of one to a few pixels around very bright sources) is well documented in the broader nighttime-lights literature associated with the Earth Observation Group (e.g. work by C. Elvidge and colleagues on VIIRS DNB characterisation) [verify -- a specific paper and exact spread-distance figure were not independently re-confirmed against a primary source in this research pass].
evidence.study_area_of_that_work: The two official VIIRS Earth Engine products are global, general-purpose composites, not built or validated for any specific city or lake-monitoring use case. The harmonized 1992-2023 dataset is likewise a global product, developed and validated using global DMSP/VIIRS overlap data, not calibrated or tested against Indian or Bengaluru-specific conditions. Neither work is scoped to small urban lakes or to a 30 m buffer question of any kind.
evidence.applies_to_indian_urban_lakes: No application of VIIRS nighttime lights specifically to Bengaluru lake-encroachment monitoring, at any spatial scale, was confirmed during this research pass. Nighttime-lights-based urban growth studies exist broadly for Indian cities at a coarse, city-wide scale, but a lake- or buffer-specific Bengaluru application was not located [uncertain -- an exhaustive literature search could not be completed in this research pass because the web-search tool's budget was exhausted partway through and only targeted document fetches remained available].
evidence.evidence_recency: 2024 for the harmonized simulated dataset (Chen et al., Scientific Data); the two official VIIRS products are actively maintained with the annual product's documented coverage extending through January 2025 and the monthly product through mid-2026, both confirmed directly from their Earth Engine catalogue pages in this research pass. The core evidence supporting this item is therefore current, not dependent on pre-2020 work.
evidence.primary_sources: NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/ANNUAL_V22 Earth Engine catalogue page: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/NOAA_VIIRS_DNB_ANNUAL_V22 (fetched and confirmed: 463.83 m resolution, bands, annual-median compositing method, cf_cvg quality-flag guidance). NOAA/VIIRS/DNB/MONTHLY_V1/VCMCFG Earth Engine catalogue page: https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/NOAA_VIIRS_DNB_MONTHLY_V1_VCMCFG (fetched and confirmed: 463.83 m resolution, stray-light/lunar/cloud filtering, Version 1's lack of aurora/fire/boat filtering). Chen, X. et al. (2024), 'A global annual simulated VIIRS nighttime light dataset from 1992 to 2023', Scientific Data 11:1380, doi 10.1038/s41597-024-04228-6 (fetched and confirmed: dataset name, sensors harmonized, 500 m resolution, NTLSRU-Net methodology, stated blooming/saturation/urban-core-underestimation limitations), data archive https://doi.org/10.6084/m9.figshare.22262545.v8. Lake-size figures (Sankey Tank 12.4 ha/~350 m across; Bellandur 315 ha) as given in this project's own task specification, used here only as the basis for the pixel-count-in-buffer arithmetic derived in this file, not drawn from an external source.

risk.failure_modes: (1) The fundamental, unfixable failure mode is spatial: at ~464 m per pixel, no processing choice (finer temporal compositing, harmonization, additional years of data) can shrink VIIRS's footprint down to a 30 m buffer -- this is a sensor-resolution limit, not a methodological one, and no amount of additional engineering resolves it. (2) Blooming/overglow from Bengaluru's very bright IT-corridor and Outer Ring Road commercial cores -- several of which sit near the project's own lakes (Bellandur, Varthur) -- will bleed into any coarser ward/catchment aggregate, making it hard to attribute a rising radiance trend specifically to development pressure near a given lake rather than to generic city-wide brightening or a bright new development a kilometre or more away. (3) VIIRS DNB coverage begins in April 2012, so any claim about earlier years in the study window (none apply here since the study window is 2019-2025, entirely within VIIRS coverage) would require the harmonized/simulated product, which carries its own documented urban-core-underestimation and dim-pixel-recovery limitations. (4) The monthly VCMCFG product's Version 1 status (no filtering of boats, fires, or other transient lights) risks injecting noise unrelated to genuine urban pressure if monthly-resolution analysis is attempted near any lake with boat traffic, nearby fires, or festival/temporary lighting events.
risk.panel_defensibility: A panel will very quickly ask exactly the question this item was set up to answer honestly: 'how many VIIRS pixels are actually inside your buffer?' The defensible answer, computed directly above from the dataset's own confirmed 463.83 m resolution and the project's own stated lake sizes, is: essentially none -- less than one-sixth of a pixel's worth of area for the smallest lake, and still less than one full pixel's worth of area even for the largest lake (Bellandur) in the study. Presenting this null result plainly, with the arithmetic shown, is a far stronger position than attempting to report a buffer-scale nighttime-lights 'trend' that is, on inspection, actually an artefact of pixel geometry rather than a real localized signal.
risk.honest_expectation: At the 30 m buffer scale the project's evaluation is actually built around, VIIRS nighttime lights provide zero usable signal -- this is a clean, reportable null result, not a shortcoming of the analysis. At ward or catchment scale, VIIRS could plausibly support a coarse, city-level contextual narrative about general development pressure trending upward around a lake's broader neighbourhood over time, but even that reading is confounded by overglow from unrelated bright developments in the same ward and can never be tied to the specific 30 m legal buffer line being tested. It should be used, if at all, as a labelled contextual side-note, never as quantitative evidence bearing on the encroachment question at the scale the project needs.

verdict.recommended_rank: reject for the buffer-scale question as the project actually specifies it (30 m); consider-with-reasons only as an explicitly-labelled, ward/catchment-scale contextual narrative that is never conflated with buffer-scale evidence, and only if the student has spare time after higher-value items -- the resolution mismatch computed here is a physical sensor limit, not something implementation effort can fix.
verdict.one_line_for_the_guide: VIIRS nighttime lights are a genuinely year-varying urbanisation proxy, but at roughly 464 m per pixel even our largest lake's 30 m legal buffer contains less than one full pixel, so we did not use it as buffer-scale evidence and would only ever present it, clearly labelled, as an unverified ward-level contextual note.
